gloss_terse: Field, cultivated terrain; used of terraced agricultural land in poetic and prophetic descriptions of fertility or devastation.
gloss_readable: A feminine noun appearing only in the plural, denoting cultivated fields or terraced agricultural land. In Deuteronomy 32:32 it describes the vine-fields of Sodom, while Isaiah 16:8 laments the famed fields of Heshbon. Habakkuk 3:17 pairs it with the failure of the fig tree and vine, painting a picture of total agricultural collapse. The word carries a sense of carefully worked terrain, land shaped by human labor, which makes its destruction all the more poignant in prophetic judgment oracles.

senses.1: Cultivated field or terraced agricultural land, always plural in Biblical Hebrew. The Spanish 'campos' and English 'fields' confirm the straightforward agricultural sense. Used both of literal farmland (Deut 32:32, 2 Kgs 23:4) and poetically of productive terrain whose devastation signals divine judgment (Isa 16:8; Hab 3:17). The Jeremiah 31:40 reference designates a specific locale near Jerusalem.

gloss_terse: Shur — a region on the southwestern border of Canaan near Egypt, associated with wilderness travel and the patriarchal narratives.
gloss_readable: A proper noun designating a region in the northeastern Sinai, along the southwestern border of Canaan and the eastern frontier of Egypt. Shur appears in connection with Hagar's flight (Gen 16:7, 'the road to Shur'), Abraham's sojourning territory (Gen 20:1), and the boundary marker for Ishmaelite territory (Gen 25:18). After the Exodus, Israel entered the 'wilderness of Shur' (Exod 15:22). The name may derive from a word meaning 'wall,' possibly referencing an Egyptian line of border fortifications across the Suez isthmus, though this remains debated.

senses.1: Shur, a geographic region on the eastern border of Egypt and southwestern edge of Canaan. The consistent transliteration across languages (Spanish 'Shur,' French 'Schur/Shur,' German 'Schur') reflects its status as a fixed proper noun. It functions as both a directional landmark ('the way to Shur,' Gen 16:7) and a wilderness designation ('wilderness of Shur,' Exod 15:22), marking the liminal space between Egypt and the promised land in patriarchal and exodus narratives.

gloss_terse: Black, dark-colored; used of hair, horses, and skin complexion in ritual, prophetic, and poetic texts.
gloss_readable: An adjective meaning 'black' or 'dark,' applied to physical color in three distinct contexts. In Leviticus 13:31 and 13:37, priestly law uses it to assess hair color in skin-disease diagnosis — black hair signals health. Song of Solomon employs it both for the beloved's self-description ('I am dark,' 1:5) and for the lover's locks ('his locks are black,' 5:11). Zechariah's vision features black horses (6:2, 6:6) as agents of divine purpose. The Spanish 'morena' for Song 1:5 captures the warmth of the term better than a stark 'black,' hinting at sun-darkened beauty rather than mere color.

senses.1: Black or dark in color, describing observable physical appearance. The Spanish rendering 'morena' (Song 1:5) versus 'negro' (Lev 13:31) reveals a semantic nuance: the word covers both neutral color description (hair in priestly diagnosis, Lev 13:31, 37; horses in prophetic vision, Zech 6:2, 6) and an aesthetically charged darkness (the beloved's sun-kissed complexion, Song 1:5; the lover's raven hair, Song 5:11). All uses share the core denotation of dark coloring.

gloss_terse: To spread out, spread abroad; stretching something flat over an open area, used literally of drying and figuratively of divine expansion.
gloss_readable: A verb meaning to spread out or stretch something flat across an open surface. Its most vivid use is in Numbers 11:32, where the Israelites spread out quail around the camp to dry them — the Vulgate's 'siccaverunt' confirms the drying purpose. In 2 Samuel 17:19 the woman of Bahurim spreads grain over a well to conceal Jonathan and Ahimaaz. The Piel intensification appears in Psalm 88:9 of spreading out hands in prayer. Job 12:23 offers a striking figurative extension: God 'spreads out' the nations, expanding their territory before bringing them low.

senses.1: To spread out flat, stretch abroad over an open area. The Spanish 'esparcirán' (scatter) and 'extiende' (extend) capture the two poles of the verb's range: dispersing objects across space (Num 11:32, spreading quail to dry; Jer 8:2, bones spread before sun and moon) and extending or stretching something (2 Sam 17:19, covering spread over a well; Job 12:23, God expanding nations). The Piel form in Psalm 88:9 adds intensity to the gesture of spreading out hands in desperate prayer.

gloss_terse: To bear a grudge, cherish animosity; persistent hostile feeling that may erupt into persecution.
gloss_readable: A verb expressing deep-seated, enduring hostility — not a momentary flash of anger but a settled disposition of enmity. Esau's grudge against Jacob after losing the blessing (Gen 27:41) provides the paradigmatic use: sustained animosity born of personal injury. Joseph's brothers fear this same smoldering resentment (Gen 50:15). In the Psalms and Job, the verb shifts to describe relentless persecution: the psalmist's enemies hate him 'with angry fury' (Ps 55:4), and Job accuses God of turning persecutor (Job 16:9; 30:21). The German gloss's struggle to translate this word highlights its specificity — it is more than simple hatred; it is grudge-bearing with intent.

senses.1: To harbor persistent enmity, bear a grudge, or cherish animosity against someone. Possibly related to the root behind 'satan' (adversary), suggesting a disposition of opposition. The Spanish 'aborreció' (loathed) and French 'haïr' (hate) approximate the meaning, but the Hebrew carries a particular nuance of sustained, smoldering hostility. Used of Esau against Jacob (Gen 27:41), Joseph's brothers' fear of retaliation (Gen 49:23; 50:15), and Job's anguished perception of divine persecution (Job 16:9; 30:21). Psalm 55:4 adds the element of angry fury accompanying the grudge.

gloss_terse: To accuse, act as adversary; denominative from 'satan,' describing the role of legal or spiritual opposition.
gloss_readable: A denominative verb from the noun 'satan' (adversary), meaning to act as an accuser or opponent. All six occurrences cluster in the Psalms and Zechariah, painting a courtroom-like scene of accusation. In Zechariah 3:1, the Satan stands at the right hand of Joshua the high priest 'to accuse him' — the infinitive construct captures the purposeful, adversarial stance. The Psalms use it of human enemies who repay good with accusation (Ps 109:4) and who function as hostile prosecutors (Ps 71:13; 109:20, 29). The consistent Spanish 'adversarios' and English 'accusers' confirm the legal-forensic register of this verb.

senses.1: To act as an adversary, accuse, or oppose in a quasi-legal sense. Derived from the noun 'satan' (adversary/accuser), this verb carries forensic overtones of formal opposition. The Spanish 'adversarios' and French 'accuser' preserve the courtroom flavor. In Zechariah 3:1, the infinitive 'to accuse him' describes the Satan's prosecutorial role before the divine tribunal. The Psalms deploy it for human enemies who relentlessly oppose the righteous: they are 'my accusers' (Ps 71:13; 109:20, 29), and their hostility replaces the love the psalmist showed them (Ps 109:4; cf. Ps 38:20).

gloss_terse: Flood, torrent, overwhelming rush of water; used literally of rainstorms and figuratively of divine wrath or calamity.
gloss_readable: A masculine noun denoting a sudden, overwhelming rush of water — a flash flood or torrent. Job 38:25 uses it literally of the channel God carves for the thunderstorm's deluge. But the word's most powerful appearances are figurative: Nahum 1:8 warns that God will make a complete end of his adversaries 'with an overflowing flood,' while Daniel 9:26 and 11:22 deploy it for armies that sweep through like floodwaters. Proverbs 27:4 pairs it with anger — 'a flood of fury' — capturing unbridled emotional force. The French 'inondation' and Spanish 'inundación' preserve both the literal and overwhelming-force dimensions.

senses.1: A flood, torrent, or overwhelming rush of water, both literal and metaphorical. The Spanish 'inundación' and French 'inondation' confirm the core meaning of sudden inundation. Job 38:25 presents the literal sense: God directing the channel for the rain-torrent. Figuratively, it conveys irresistible destructive force — divine judgment sweeping away enemies (Nah 1:8), invading armies overwhelming a land (Dan 9:26; 11:22), and uncontrollable fury (Prov 27:4, 'a flood of anger'). Psalm 32:6 uses it as warning: pray before the flood of great waters rises too high.

gloss_terse: The Shilonite — a gentilic adjective identifying someone from Shiloh, applied especially to the prophet Ahijah.
gloss_readable: A gentilic adjective meaning 'the one from Shiloh,' used almost exclusively to identify the prophet Ahijah who prophesied the division of Solomon's kingdom. The definite article is consistently attached — 'the Shilonite' — marking it as a recognized epithet. Five of the six occurrences refer to Ahijah (1 Kgs 11:29; 12:15; 15:29; 2 Chr 9:29; 10:15), while 1 Chronicles 9:5 uses the term collectively for inhabitants of Shiloh who settled in Jerusalem after the exile. The spelling varies slightly between Kings and Chronicles, reflecting normal orthographic fluidity in Hebrew proper adjectives.

senses.1: Gentilic adjective meaning 'the Shilonite,' designating a person from the ancient Israelite sanctuary city of Shiloh. The Spanish 'el shilonita/el silonita' and French 'le Shilonite' preserve the gentilic function. Primarily an epithet for the prophet Ahijah, who announced the northern kingdom's secession to Jeroboam (1 Kgs 11:29) and whose word was fulfilled in the division (1 Kgs 12:15; 15:29; 2 Chr 9:29). In 1 Chronicles 9:5, it refers collectively to descendants of Shiloh who resettled in Jerusalem.

gloss_terse: Bereaved, robbed of offspring; describing a mother — animal or human — deprived of her young, fierce in grief.
gloss_readable: An adjective describing one robbed of offspring, carrying powerful emotional force. Its most memorable usage is the simile of the bereaved bear — a mother bear stripped of her cubs becomes ferociously dangerous (2 Sam 17:8; Hos 13:8; Prov 17:12). Hushai warns Absalom that David's men are 'as fierce as a bear robbed of her cubs,' and Proverbs declares it better to meet such a bear than a fool in his folly. In Song of Solomon 4:2 and 6:6, the image softens strikingly: ewes from the washing, 'none bereaved' — every ewe paired with twin lambs, a picture of perfect fertility and completeness.

senses.1: Bereaved or deprived of offspring, describing both animals and humans who have lost their young. The Spanish 'privada de crías' (deprived of offspring) captures the sense precisely. Three occurrences form the iconic simile of the bereaved bear, ferocious in maternal grief (2 Sam 17:8; Prov 17:12; Hos 13:8). Song of Solomon uses the negation — 'none bereaved among them' — to paint a picture of complete fruitfulness among the flock (Song 4:2; 6:6). Jeremiah 18:21 applies it to human mothers in a devastating imprecation.

gloss_terse: Shammai — a personal name in the tribe of Judah, borne by three men in the Chronicler's genealogies.
gloss_readable: A proper masculine noun naming three distinct individuals in the genealogies of Judah recorded in 1 Chronicles. The first Shammai is the son of Onam and brother of Jada (1 Chr 2:28, 32), the second is the son of Rekem in a Calebite line (1 Chr 2:44-45), and the third appears as a son of Mered in a Judahite sub-clan (1 Chr 4:17). The LXX renders the name variously as Sammai, Sammei, and Sami, while the German gloss 'mein Name' appears to be an etymological reading connecting it to the root 'shem' (name). All occurrences are confined to the Chronicler's tribal records.

senses.1: Shammai, a personal name borne by three men in the tribe of Judah. The English 'Shamai' and Spanish 'Samay' transliterate the name, while the German 'mein-Name' reflects a folk etymology from 'shem' (name). The first Shammai is son of Onam in the line of Jerahmeel (1 Chr 2:28, 32); the second descends from Caleb through Rekem (1 Chr 2:44-45); the third belongs to a Judahite sub-clan through Mered (1 Chr 4:17). All references appear in the Chronicler's genealogical records establishing tribal heritage.
